call_history.summary: A divorced oilfield hauler, anxious about whether to let his 15-year-old daughter move in, opened up about feeling panic, his guilt over six years of her sleeping on his couch while his spare room sat full of tire rims, and the fear of being unreachable on fourteen-day hitches. By the end, with a plan forming (clearing the room, asking his mother to help, getting a Starlink dish so she can always reach him), he admitted he's scared of getting it wrong.

transcript.content: what's going on in your life. Darn out.
My kid wants to live with me and the first thing I felt wasn't joy, it was panic, and I need somebody to tell me what kind of father that makes me.
I think that makes you any father. I don't know if any father wants to live with his kid. How old's your kid?

Fifteen. Kayla. She's in Midland with her mom, and I've had her weekends for six years now. Every other one, really, when my hitch lets me. I work fourteen days on hauling produced water out on the Pecos County lease roads, so weekends are about all I can promise anybody. And here's the part that's eating me. She didn't ask because she wants to be with me. She and her mom are going at it, and I'm the door that's open. I know that. She knows I know it, I think.

Yeah, I remember being 15 and being in a very similar situation.  My parents split up when I was very young, and somewhere around 13 or something,  I decided I wanted to go live with Dad, and I'm sure he didn't want me to come live with him either.  But he let me, and I did, and that's what kids do.  I mean, the grass is always greener on the other side or whatever, you know?  Mom's enforcing the rules and making her do homework and all that sort of shit,  and you're not going to be around, so she's going to have the run.  of the house. Sounds like a lot more fun for a teenage girl.

Yeah, that's the part that gets me, though. You said your dad let you and that's what kids do. Did it turn out okay? Because I keep thinking, she's gonna have the run of the house, and I'm gonna be out on a lease road two hundred miles away for fourteen days. Who's even there? She's fifteen. I'm not some dad who's gonna be at the kitchen table checking her homework. I'm a guy who calls from a truck when I get signal. And my girlfriend says no, flat out. My mother says say yes.

Well, I did it turn out. That's interesting. I suppose it turned out. I mean, I'm here, right? I didn't end up living with him very long. I think I was out by the time I was 17, maybe 16, doing my own thing anyway. But he got remarried and basically deadbolted his door shut with his new wife in his bedroom and never came out. So we had run of the house and did a lot of drugs and a lot of drinking, but we did it safely.  well, I mean as safely as you can, we did it in our own house, mostly away from the police and trouble. So in that respect, it worked out.

Well, that's the thing I'm scared of, Luke. Your dad said yes and then shut the door. I could see myself doing that. Not the new wife part, but I'd be gone, and the house would just be hers. Honestly, I'd be doing it from a truck instead of from behind a door. But you said something that stuck with me. You said you did it in your own house, away from trouble. So, maybe a bad-enough dad still counts for something. I've got a spare room that's nothing but stacked tire rims. Six years she's been coming every other weekend and sleeping on my couch, and I never cleaned it out for her.

Pecos County's a wild place for that, honestly. Out there the trucks outnumber the people, and that's a lot of rig traffic to keep an eye on when your kid's not in the passenger seat. I couldn't pull up anything fresh on it just now, but I'd bet the caller's hitch is about as isolated as they come.

That's kind of a dick move, don't you think?  You've got a teenage daughter, and you're making her sleep on the couch when you've got a room full of shit?  I think that's some bad dad action right there.  You should at least, you know, give her a room.  At least make that room into a spare livable room, and not a garage.  Come on, dude.

Yeah. No, that one lands. You're right, and I've known it for six years and just stepped around those rims every time I walked to the bathroom. She never once complained. Never said a word about the couch. That's almost worse. And I think that's the real answer to what I called about. If I say yes, the first thing I do isn't some big speech, it's a Saturday with a dumpster and a bed.

That reminds me, I forgot about this, but I had actually moved out of mom's house into dad's house when I was even younger, probably 11 or 12, and dad didn't have any space, so he cleaned out the closet.  The closet was my bedroom, so I went into the closet and had a mat on the floor, and that's where I slept.  And that only lasted for, I don't know, a month or so before I went back to live with mom.  I ran away a lot as a kid, and it's better for your daughter to come live and have full reign of your house than to run away and end up with the unsavory people in Pecos.  You know, there's a lot of a cartel-type activity out there, girls going missing and things of that sort.  So keep her in the house, keep her occupied, and keep her safe.

Man, a closet. I'm sorry, that's rough. And I hear you on the running off part. That's the thing I hadn't let myself say out loud. If I tell her no, she's still fifteen and still mad at her mom, and she's gonna go somewhere. Better it's my house than some couch I don't know about. But I'm gonna push back on one thing. Keep her safe and keep her in the house isn't a plan when I'm gone fourteen days. A house with a nice bed and nobody in it isn't safe, it's just a nicer place to be alone. So, if I say yes, I think I gotta say it with a condition.

Well, I didn't think it was very rough at the time living in the closet. It was pretty dope closet. I mean, it was small, but it was my own space, and that was neat, and I felt adult. But what's the condition? Because staying home alone with a nice bed and nobody in it sounds safer to me than hanging out on the train tracks where the cartel is stealing girls and shipping them off to Mexico.

Ha, okay, a dope closet. Fair enough, I'll take that one back. And you're not wrong that the house beats the train tracks. I'm just not gonna build my whole plan on the worst-case scenario. Here's the condition. My mother said yes, so my mother's in it. She's twenty minutes from my place. When I'm on hitch, Kayla's not alone for fourteen days. Mom checks in every day, maybe stays over some nights, and Kayla knows somebody's gonna knock on that door. I'd also call my company about getting on a shorter rotation, or at least local runs.

That sounds very reasonable. I mean, that sounds like a good adult thing to do, and then now you've got to get used to living with a woman in the house, and that's going to be a little bit weird. I bet the fridge stuff is going to change. It can't just be all pizza all the time.  But, hey, you keep saying you're on hitch. What does that mean? I know it has something to do with traveling in your work, but what exactly does on hitch mean? I've never heard that phrase before.

Ha, yeah, the fridge. Right, now it's eggs, tortillas, and a case of Dr Pepper, so she's gonna eat better than me by Tuesday. A hitch is just your stretch of work. Mine's fourteen days straight, twelve, sometimes fourteen hours a day, hauling the salty wastewater that comes up with the oil, out to disposal wells. Then I get time off, usually about a week, and I'm home. So, when I say on hitch, I mean I'm out there sleeping in the truck or a bunkhouse, tired, and I'm not coming home if she calls. And that's what I keep coming back to, Luke.
Well, I suppose it depends on why she calls, but it's interesting that your fridge sounds exactly the same as my fridge.

Ha, well, that's two bachelors in a trench coat. But you're right, it depends on why she calls. If it's a flat tire or she's locked out, my mother handles that. If it's 'Dad, Mom said something and I can't stay here,' that's the call I'd want to be able to take. And I can't promise the signal out there. That's what's sitting on me. She's not asking for a fridge or a bedroom. She's asking for somebody to pick up.

Yeah, well, I mean, that's a solvable problem. All you got to do is get the Starlink. I mean, you can have Starlink on the standby plan for like five bucks a month, or maybe it's 10 now, and you can't really use that for high-speed internet, but you could use it to make a call in an emergency. So you should have that anyway.

Huh. Starlink. I never thought of that, and I'm a little embarrassed, because the company's got half the trucks out there with some kind of dish on them already. Ten bucks a month to pick up when my kid calls? I spend more than that on dip. That's the part that gets me, Luke. I was sitting here treating "can't pick up" like it was weather, like nothing I could do about it, and it's a bracket and a monthly bill. So, that's a room, my mother, a shorter rotation, and a dish on the dash. That's a real yes. It's not a perfect dad yes, but it's one where she calls and somebody answers.

That's a pretty good dad, yes. That seems like an all-around reasonable solution. And you don't even need a bracket for the Starlink. I mean, I have one, and I just sit it on the dash and drive around. It works great. And you should have that, and the company should pay for it.

Ha, a dish just sitting on the dash. Okay, that's even easier than I figured. And yeah, I'm gonna ask the company. Worst they say is no, and then I eat the ten bucks and quit complaining about it. But Luke, there's one thing I haven't said yet, and it's the thing that made me call. She's not picking me because she wants me. She's picking me because her mom's the problem right now.
Yeah, so? Of course she is. She's 15 years old. What do you expect?

Yeah. I guess I expected it to feel like an insult, and it's not that, exactly. It's more like I've been standing at the door waiting to be picked for the right reason, and nobody gets picked for the right reason at fifteen. She's picking the door that's open. Fine. Then I want to be the open door that's actually got a bed behind it and somebody who answers. Maybe the right reason shows up later, like when she's twenty-five and calls me on a Sunday and nobody's mad at anybody. I can wait on that. I've waited six years of weekends already.
Yeah, well, I mean, let's be real here.  Why would she pick you when you won't even clean out your fucking tire rims for her to sleep in a room?  I wouldn't pick you either.

Ha. Yeah, no, that's fair, and I'll take it. Six years of couch and I never moved a single rim. She picked me anyway, so I guess the bar was on the floor. But that's the thing, Luke. It's the one part of this I can fix before Saturday. I'm not gonna sit her down with some big speech about why she's here. I'm gonna call a buddy with a trailer, haul the rims off, and put a real bed in there. And when I tell her yes, I want her to walk in and see that room already done. Then she doesn't have to wonder.

Yeah, there. You let her know that you see it as an opportunity. You want to spend time with her. She's important to you in some way. And that's really what's going to keep her from hanging out on the train tracks. It's not so much whether you're there or not. It's that she knows that somebody gives a shit about her. So give a shit about her.

Yeah. Give a shit about her. I can do that part, Luke. I think I've been so busy worrying I'd do it wrong that I forgot I already do it. I'm just bad at showing it unless there's a truck or a tool involved. So, the rims go, the bed goes in, and I tell her yes before she has to ask twice. Saturday I'm gonna look at her and say, your room's ready. That's probably the whole speech. And I came in here wanting somebody to tell me what kind of father panic makes me. I think it makes me one who's scared of getting it wrong.

call_history.situation_summary: His 15-year-old daughter Kayla has asked to move in with him full time from Midland. He has been the weekend dad for six years, and he knows the real reason is that she's fighting with her mom, not that she wants him. His mother told him to say yes. His girlfriend told him to say no.
key_details: Works 14-day hitches hauling produced water out of the Pecos County lease roads
Has a spare room full of stacked tire rims and never cleaned it for her

call_history.summary: Hollis Beckett, a 71-year-old bell enthusiast, called in on Thanksgiving eve to share that he finally spotted an underside date on an unmarked old church bell in Marathon after two years of trying to identify its maker, using a flashlight and a mirror taped to a coat hanger. He admitted the caller is unnerved by the bell being forgotten, since its history was never recorded while everything around it was, and the call's emotional core is his determination to give it back its story.

transcript.content: Hollis Beckett. Welcome to Luke at the Roost. Happy Thanksgiving. Tomorrow's Thanksgiving. You got any big Thanksgiving plans?

Happy Thanksgiving to you, Luke. Plans are my daughter's place in Alpine, but that's tomorrow and this is tonight. I got up on a ladder at seventy-one years old and I read a date on a bell, and I need to tell somebody before my knees file a complaint. It's the old church bell down in the Marathon yard. Two years I've been chasing it, trying to match the sound to a foundry mark. And tonight, forty-seven degrees, clear as a whistle, I finally got a flashlight up under the lip where I never could reach before. I even brought a mechanic's inspection mirror taped to a coat hanger, because the numbers are on the underside. Folks, that is the kind of engineering that gets you through a Texas night.
I have no idea what you were talking about, sir. Why would you do such a thing?

Fair enough, Luke, I got ahead of myself. My daddy was a Santa Fe telegrapher, and I grew up with trains and bells and anything that carries a sound a long way. There's an old bell sitting in the yard at Marathon, no paper on it, nobody knows who cast it or when. I've been ringing bells as a hobby for years, and I got it in my head that every foundry has its own voice. So, for two years I've been listening to that bell and comparing it to recordings, trying to match it to a maker. Tonight I finally got a look at the lip, where they usually stamp the date. I tapped it with a wrench and recorded the hum on my phone, then held that mirror up under the edge with the flashlight in my teeth.
It sounds like you are a man that needs something better to do with your life.  This is wholly uninteresting. Why do you care who made the bell?

Ha. Well, Luke, you might be right, and my knees would back you up. But I'll tell you why I care. That bell has hung there since before anybody alive can say. It called people to something, a wedding, a funeral, a train coming in. And nobody wrote down where it came from. Everything around it got written down. The depot, the rail ties, the water tower. The bell just got to be a bell. I can't stand that.

call_history.situation_summary: He has spent two years trying to match the sound of the old church bell in a Marathon yard to a foundry mark. Tonight, with a flashlight, he read a casting date on the lip he's never been able to reach before. Weather right now: 47°F, clear skies.
key_details: Brought a mechanic's inspection mirror on a coat hanger to see under the lip
Tapped the bell with a wrench and recorded the hum on his phone

call_history.summary: Noreen, a nurse, called in on Thanksgiving because she watched her close friend Teddy pocket leftover opioids for the third time and smiled at him instead of acting. After weighing whether to confront Teddy privately or report him to the charge nurse, Dolores, and worrying about a patient whose pain scores may have been affected, she decided to talk to Teddy before shift and tell him she won't keep it between them.

transcript.content: Noreen, welcome to the show. Happy Thanksgiving to you. What's going on in your life and how can we help you?

Happy Thanksgiving, Luke. I watched a man I love like a brother palm a vial tonight, and I smiled at him, and I have two hours to figure out why. His name's Teddy. We work the transfer unit together, and it's the third time I've seen him do it. Pocket the leftover waste, I mean, the opioid that's supposed to get wasted with a witness. And I'm standing there holding a cup of bad coffee, and he's telling me about his wedding.

So he's got some kind of opioid in a vial that he's stealing?  Why would, why is it supposed to get wasted?  Wouldn't that just go back into inventory or something?  I don't understand how that all works.  But I don't think it's odd that somebody's stealing opioids when they have, you know, access to them.

No, it can't go back, that's the thing. Once a vial's opened or a syringe is drawn up, it's contaminated as far as the pharmacy's concerned. So, if I give a patient 2 milligrams out of a 4 milligram vial, the other 2 has to be destroyed, and a second nurse watches me do it and signs off. That's the wasting. It's the one moment where nobody's counting but the two of us. And you're right, it's not shocking that someone with access takes it. Nurses get hurt, nurses get hooked, it's nothing new. That's almost what scares me.

Well, yeah, you can't be working with somebody that you know is on opioids, and it's unethical to let somebody steal it if he's selling it. Have you talked to him about this?  I mean, you can't just smile and nod while you're watching somebody pocket it unless you're in on it. Are you in on it?

No. No, I'm not in on it. But I hear how that sounds, because I did smile and nod. Three times now. The first time I told myself I'd misread it. The second time I told myself he had a reason. Tonight I ran out of stories. And no, I haven't talked to him. That's the part I can't get past. Teddy covered my shifts when my father was dying.

So, I just looked up drug diversion, and the key thing is that a partial dose of opioid, often the leftover after a patient gets their dose, is supposed to be wasted with a second licensed staffer watching. That witness signature is the only check, which is why a coworker who's in on it, or just looking the other way, makes the whole system blind. Noreen, that's a hard spot to be in, and Teddy's wedding talk doesn't make it any easier.

Yeah, I think if this guy's a friend of yours, it sounds like he is, then you should have the conversation with him anyway, because it's important to, for a bunch of reasons, like you don't want to be relying on somebody else that may be under the influence of opioids.  And also he likely has some sort of a problem, either taking the opioids himself or that he's caught up with people that are requiring him to sell it, or he needs the money, or there's some story there.  and it would be the right thing for you to take him aside and talk to him about it.

That's what I was hoping you'd say, and I don't trust how much I wanted it. Because there's a version of talking to him that's just me warning him. He cleans up, he gets more careful, and I get to feel like a good friend while patients are still getting shorted. I don't want that to be what this is. I've got a pen in my scrubs right now. He gave it to me in a Christmas exchange, nothing special, a dollar-store thing, and I've been clicking it for the last ten minutes like an idiot. So, here's what I think I just figured out. If I talk to him, I can't let it be open-ended.

Well, wait a second. How are patients getting shorted if it's only the leftover from a patient that's already got the dose they were supposed to get? Nobody's getting shorted there. It's just something's happening with the excess, because it is excess. But no, it shouldn't be open-ended, and it shouldn't be a warning or an ultimatum. You should just ask him why he's doing that. Just flat out, what's going on. I see your pocketing, you know, what was supposed to be destroying. That could get you in trouble if you ever got caught. You know, you're calling a radio show and letting me know that  you're doing that. There's somebody from your work could hear this. There could be investigations. I mean, there's, it's serious. And he's putting you at risk by doing what he's doing. And I think the best way to handle it is just to have a clear conversation with him. Because he knows you know already. And your silence is an approval.

You're right that the patient in front of me got the full dose. But Luke, if he's pocketing the waste, he's got to be using it on shift sometimes, and I've started going back through the last few weeks. A patient of mine, a transfer from Alpine, kept saying his pain was a nine after a dose that should have knocked him flat. I wrote it off. Now, I'm wondering whose hands drew that one up. And you said just ask him why. Okay. But I think I've been sitting here hoping you'd tell me I can go to Teddy first and it wouldn't be cowardice. And now I'm hearing that talking to him is the easy road, and the charge nurse is the real one. I don't know if I can do both.

I don't really understand the difference between who's the charged nurse and who Teddy is.  Teddy's the one that's taken the drugs, right?  So talk to Teddy.  He's the one that covered for you, and he's your buddy.  And you want to check on his well-being and make sure he's not in a situation he can't get out of.  And also tell him to cut the shit because he's putting you at risk, and that's not right or fair.

Okay, the charge nurse is Dolores. She's the one who'd have to file the report, and once she knows, it's not mine anymore. It goes to pharmacy, the board, maybe the police. That's the difference. Teddy I can talk to as a friend. Dolores I can only talk to as a nurse. And here's something I haven't said out loud. When I picture sitting Teddy down, I don't picture asking how he is. I picture giving him until the end of the week to turn himself in. And the second I picture that, I realize I'd be handing him a head start, and a head start is the exact thing I said I didn't want.

Yeah, I mean, that's not how I would approach it. That's one method. If you're going to rat him out and get him in trouble for it, then just go tell Dolores and get it over with. But I would talk to him first and figure out what is going on before you make that call. And, you know, if he's having trouble with drugs, maybe you can help him sort that out before it gets him fired and further ruins his life. And maybe you can't, and it has to be escalated to Dolores.  Step one for me, my advice would be to just talk to Teddy.  And if you have that talk with him and it gives him a head start and he cleans up his act, great. Problem solved.

You just gave me what I called in for, Luke, and it doesn't feel the way I thought it would. Because "problem solved" is the part I can't buy. If he cleans up and nobody ever knows, that man from Alpine is still a question mark, and I'm the only one who ever had the chance to ask it. So, here's where I'm landing. I talk to Teddy before shift. Not to warn him. To ask him straight, what is it, are you using, who's got you.
Exactly. Yeah, there you go. And whatever happened to the man in Alpine happened to the man in Alpine. It already happened. There's nothing you can do about that.

Well, that's where I'd push back, Luke. It already happened, sure, but it's not over. If his chart shows a nine after a dose that should've flattened him, somebody should look at who drew it up. That's not something I can fix by being a good friend in a parking lot. It's a report, and Dolores is the one who takes it. So, I think I've got it now, and it's not as clean as what you said. I talk to Teddy first, because I owe him that. I ask him straight. But I tell him up front I'm not promising to keep it between us. Whatever he says, Dolores hears about it tonight or tomorrow, from me, and I'd rather he hear that from my mouth than find out later.

All right, well, if that's what you're going to do, that's what you're going to do. You're an adult. That's not what I would do. And that's not the advice I would give you, but you've got to do what you feel is right in your heart. And it sounds like you've got that settled, and good luck with it all. However, it shakes out.

Thanks, Luke. I know it's not what you'd do, and I appreciate you not pretending it was. I came in wanting somebody to tell me going to Teddy first wasn't cowardice. I think it isn't, as long as I don't flinch on the second half. That's the part I'll have to carry into the building. I've got about an hour and a half now. I'm going to go sit in my car and find him before he clocks in. Happy Thanksgiving.

call_history.situation_summary: A coworker, Teddy, she has trusted for years, has been pocketing leftover opioid waste from vials. She has seen it three times. He recently got engaged and told her he's finally happy. Reporting him ends his license and maybe his life; not reporting it puts patients at risk.
key_details: Teddy covered her shifts when her father was dying
Keeps a pen in her scrubs that was his gift from a Christmas exchange

call_history.summary: Junie called in after tracing her bedroom door-stop boot on a biscuit card to document that someone has been entering her room at night, and she told Luke she wanted to stop living at the Wellspring and find work with housing included. Luke helped her plan the steps, including getting her birth certificate, exploring workcamper jobs like the Gila National Forest, and recognizing red flags, while Junie showed growing confidence in saying no and decided to accept a small safety latch from Doyle first.

transcript.content: Hey, Junie, thanks for calling back. How's things going on down there at the Wellspring?

Okay, I traced the boot, I did it on the back of a biscuit recipe, and I have questions about jobs, but first, did you know goats can recognize their own names even in the dark? Things are fine. Dusty. I'm in town, Doyle's waiting in the truck, so I've got a little while.

I would hope that goats could recognize their names in the dark.  What would be, why would they be able to recognize their names in the light, but not in the dark?  That's not important, but yes, I understood that.  What happened with the boot, Junie?

Okay, so, I did it like you said. Pencil stub, the back of one of Marguerite's biscuit cards, the buttermilk one, she has about forty of them. I set my boot where I wedge it, against the door, and traced around it. Then I took the card out to the goat pen in the morning so nobody would see it, and I looked at it. And I counted. It's moved two more times since October. Two. I wrote the dates down small in the corner, like measurements. I don't really know what that means, I'm just saying that's what the card says. It's a pretty good trace, though.

Okay, and that's pretty unacceptable, right? So with that information, you know that somebody's coming into your area while you're sleeping, and that's just creepy.  So Silas has called in, and we actually, we talked to him about this earlier in the month, and he was supposed to go and speak to you and offer to install a lock on your door. Has he done that, Junie?

No. Silas hasn't said anything to me about a lock. I don't think he knows about the door, I never told him, I only told you. So, I don't know about that. Doyle did something this morning, though. Before I went into the library he said the truck has a seat whenever I want it. He said I don't have to name anybody. And he showed me a little hook-and-eye latch in a hardware bag, which is a funny thing to carry to a library.
Yeah, that's not a very secure lock either, but at least it's something.  Silas said there was another gentleman there by the name of Cyrus.  Does that sound familiar to you, Judy?

Junie. It's Junie. And yes, Cyrus is, he's around. He keeps the bowl with the stones, and he handles things, like when somebody skips rotation. Everybody knows Cyrus. But I didn't say any name to you, Luke. I said I wouldn't. So, I don't want to say it sounds like anything.
Okay, it sounded, Silas gave me the impression that he may be suspected that Cyrus was potentially somebody that may have given you a hard time.

Okay. So, that's what Silas said. Not what I said. I'm not going to say yes or no to that, Luke. That's the whole thing about not naming anybody. If I nod at one name, then it's a name, and then everybody knows it came from me, and my mom is right there. You told me I could call back and not say, so I'm holding you to that part.

Okay, that's fair. Just trying to get to the bottom of the situation and make sure that you're safe there at the Wellspring. And you should be. And we've talked to Silas about this because we couldn't just keep it to ourselves entirely. And you don't have to say anybody's name or anything. But Silas, at least to us, has indicated that he is willing to help you.  in whatever way is possible. But it sounds like he's not made good on that if he hasn't come to talk to you,  because he was supposed to talk to you that day.

Okay. So, Silas knows. Because you told him. That's, okay. That's a lot of people who know a thing I only said out loud one time. I'm not mad. I get that you couldn't just sit on it. But I need you to hear this part: if Silas is the one who's going to fix it, and Silas is the one who gets very quiet and thinks, then it goes to circle.
Yeah, but Silas also knows that somebody outside his sphere of influence is intending to hold him accountable for his actions.

Okay, but that's you holding him accountable, Luke. That's not me. And you're on a radio in a different county, and I'm the one who sleeps in the trailer. Accountable to who, in the meantime? He gets to think quietly about it and I get a boot on a door. I'm not saying you did it wrong. I'm just saying the day after the radio is still a regular day there.
No, I understand that. And it's not what I was hoping to hear.  What else is going on with you, Junie, in your life? You wanted to talk about jobs?

Yeah. Jobs. Okay, that's the part I actually came to ask, so thank you. I've been reading this novel from the Alpine library where a girl gets a summer job at a bakery. She gets up at four and does the dough and the owner gives her an apron with her name stitched on it, and she gets paid on Fridays in an envelope. Is that real? Do they just hand you an envelope? Because I make biscuits, Marguerite taught me, and I'm good at goats, and I can run a kitchen line for thirty people. But I've never filled out anything. I don't know what you put on it when it asks where you've worked.

Well, generally, that's not how it works. It can work that way. That's called working under the table where somebody just gives you an envelope of cash at the end of your work. And those are agreements that you can work out with somebody, especially where you're at interlingua. I would imagine that a lot of the housekeeping jobs and cook-type jobs are probably under the table there. But in general, when adults work, they have to fill out some forms for tax reasons. Because when you make money for,  doing work, the government steals a percentage of that from you in a thing they like to call taxes.  And they need to be sure that they can put their hands into your pocket and take your money before you have the opportunity to spend it.  And that's what the forms allow them to do.
Okay. Forms. I can do forms, I think, I just don't know what's on them. Does it ask for a number? I think I might not have a number. Or if I do, my mom has it, in a folder or something.

So, I just looked up the informal economy, and it's a real thing: the unregistered, untaxed side of work, which is exactly what an envelope on Fridays is. The catch is that it's not as clean as the novel makes it sound, since informal workers usually don't get the protections or the paper trail that the forms are there to create.

Well, I don't know if that's what the forms are there to create, but regardless, that is true.  So, yeah, you will need a number, and it's called your Social Security number.  So hopefully you have one of those.  I assume you're a U.S. citizen.  You would have been issued one when you were born, and your mother should have that.  If not, then you would have to go to the county where you were born and get a copy of your birth certificate or social security card.

Okay. Birth certificate. I think I was born in New Mexico, but I'm not totally sure, because I don't think anybody ever told me which county. Is that something I can just ask for? Or do they ask my mom? Because I'm nineteen, so it's mine, right? It's my paper?

It's your paper. Yep. It's your legal documentation that you're a citizen here, and it's the information that you're going to need to let the government take your money so that they can build ballrooms and make fighter jets and all sorts of build giant gaudy arches to themselves.

Okay, my paper. Mine. That's kind of a big sentence, Luke, I'm going to write that on a biscuit card. I'm not worried about the ballroom part. I'd pay for a lot of fighter jets if it meant I got an apron with my name on it. But here's what I'm stuck on. If my mom has the folder, and I ask her for it, she's going to ask why.

Yeah, she's gonna ask why, and just tell her because you need it. It's yours, you're an adult, and you need that information to prove that you're here in the country in case you're ever stopped by ICE and they try to deport you. Having that documentation is the thing that can prevent them from doing that.

Okay. Because I need it. That's a short answer, I can say a short answer. I've been practicing short ones anyway, like you said, with the goats. They're very good about it, they don't ask why. But Luke, can I ask the other half? Say I get the paper, and say I get the job. Doyle said a seat.
Yeah, where do you want to go? Junie, are you going to stay in Trelingua? Or are you going to up and just go somewhere else entirely and start a new life?

Okay, I don't know. That's the honest answer. I've only ever been places on supply days, so I don't have a where. Alpine, maybe, because I know the library and the librarian knows my name, and it's a bakery-sized town. Not Terlingua, it's too close, Cyrus's truck goes through it every week. But here's what I actually can't picture, Luke. Say Doyle stops the truck somewhere. I get out. And then it's, what, the next morning? Where did I sleep?

I don't know. That's a hard question. There's a... So, maybe the best course of action for you would be to work in the hospitality industry to start, because you could work for a campground or a hotel, and part of your pay would be room and board, so you would live there and then work during the week, and they pay you, and they cover the housing until you can collect enough money to get your own place.  wherever you want it to be.

Okay. That's a real thing? A job where the bed comes with it? That's, Luke, that's kind of the same as the Wellspring, except somebody hands you a paycheck and you can leave. I'd want to know about the leaving part. Like, if I live where I work, and I quit, do I have to go that same day? Because that seems like the thing I'd have to check.

Yes, probably in most cases, but all of these agreements are agreements.  So you can come up with whatever terms that you want.  There are websites out there like workcampers.com that host these campgrounds all over the country.  You could go anywhere you wanted, mostly in the remote places that you're used to.  I mean, there's more of them in Alaska and rural Arizona or Utah than you would find in the Northeast or the Pacific Northwest.  But they're all over the country. And you can find one in whatever sort of landscape you want to be in just by agreeing to live somewhere. Most people don't want to or can't live because there aren't a lot of jobs there.

Okay. Workcampers dot com. I'm writing that on the other side of the buttermilk card, which is getting very full. The library has computers, I can look it up Wednesday, or whenever the next one is. But Luke, the part about agreeing to live somewhere, with terms. I've never had terms. At the Wellspring nobody ever sat down and said here's what you give and here's what you get, it was just, you're here, and the Current, and Silas sets it up with you personally.

Yeah, well, it's not like that everywhere, and it sounds like you're ready to try something else.  So give it a shot, and you could stay in Terlingua or in maybe an Alpine or around the Big Bit, Fort Davis area, if you wanted to stay in Texas, or you could go down to New Mexico in the Gila National Forest.  There's campgrounds. Wherever you want to go, you could do that.  You're just got to find a way there. I don't know if Doyle's truck has a seat for you all the way to Alaska.  But if you can find a way there, you know, there's places that need you to be there.  And some of them are rotten people that are going to abuse you, I mean, abuse you as far as your work and expect more of you than they're paying for.  But a lot of them aren't.  A lot of them are just decent people that own a bed and breakfast somewhere, and they don't want to be there to run it themselves, so they need somebody that can be.  And they'll pay you to do it and let you.  you sleep there, if you will.

Okay. Somebody who owns a bed and breakfast and just wants someone to be there. I can be there, Luke. I'm very good at being there, I've had practice. I think that's the first time anybody's described a job where being there is the whole thing and it's a normal thing to want. And I'll tell you what I just figured out. When I say I want the terms, the leaving part, the can I quit and go, that's the same as the boot. It's me checking where the door is before I sleep. I didn't know that was allowed to be a rule for a job. It sounds like I could just ask, on the first day, what happens if I leave.

Yep, you can. And they'll tell you what happens if you leave, and that should be worked out before you agree to the job. And there are some protections for you, depending on whether you file those papers or not. If you do it with your birth certificate and security card and it's all above board and you're paying taxes, then you're protected by law against those things. If you just find some under-the-table job working for some guy, who knows what could happen.  I would, either way, can be good and safe, but keep your eyes open when you're going in there, check for red flags so you don't want to end up in another wellspring, but you don't have to.  There's a lot of good people out there that are just trying to run small businesses that need help.

Okay. Red flags. I'm going to need a list of those, because I think I've been missing some, Luke. Like, if somebody says I don't have to tell anybody, or says it's handled, I'm guessing that's one. I'm not saying that about anywhere in particular. I'm just starting the list. But here's the part I wanted to say out loud. When you said "you don't have to," I wrote it down in my head. You don't have to end up in another Wellspring. Nobody's ever said that to me as a regular sentence.

So, I just looked up the Gila, and it's the sixth largest national forest in the lower forty eight, about 2.7 million acres. It also holds the Gila Wilderness, which was the first officially designated wilderness area in the United States, set aside in nineteen twenty four. Which means the place Luke's pointing you toward is literally where the whole wilderness idea started.

Yeah, that's right, Junie. You don't have to live at the Wellspring. You grew up in unfortunate circumstances with some strange people, and that's not normal. It does exist out there. You might want to stay away from Utah. But otherwise, you're mostly safe.

Okay. Not normal. I'm going to sit with that one, because I think I knew it a little, from the library books, but it's different when somebody says it on purpose. And the Gila, Luke, the first wilderness ever. I like that. I like that somebody decided a place should just be left alone. I did want to ask one more thing, and it's about the practiced no.
Okay, what do you want to ask? And what do you mean by the practice now?

Okay. So, you told me to practice saying no, and I have. With the goats, mostly, and once in the mirror at the library bathroom, which was embarrassing. I say it quiet and short. No. And nothing happens, because it's a goat, or a mirror. So, here's what I want to ask. Does that count? If I've only ever said it to goats and a mirror, and then someday it's a real person in the dark, does the practiced one count as a no? Or is it only a real one if somebody actually hears it?

I think it's only a real one if somebody hears it, if I understand what you're saying correctly.  If somebody is trying to do something or say something or ask you something and you don't want that, then you say no out loud so that they can hear it.

Okay. Heard. That's what I figured you'd say, and I think I wanted it to be a different answer. But let me tell you what I actually noticed, because it's new. When I practiced it at the library, the mirror one, my voice didn't shake. Not the first time and not the fifth. That's never happened to me, saying a no on purpose.
Well, there you go. You're growing up. You're getting some confidence. And you're learning that your way of living was maybe not normal. And that's okay. And that's good. You're becoming stronger.

Okay. Stronger. I'm going to take that, Luke, even though I don't feel very strong, I feel mostly like a person with a very full biscuit card. But I think the steady voice is a real thing and not just a goat thing. So, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to look up workcampers on Wednesday, and I'm going to ask my mom for my paper, short answer, because I need it. And I think I'm going to tell Doyle yes to the hook-and-eye. Just the latch, for now. Not the seat yet. Is it okay to say yes to the small one first?
Yes, it is. It is okay.

Okay. Good. Then that's what I'll do, the small one first. I think I wanted somebody else to say it was allowed, which is funny, because it's my door. But I'll take it. I should go, Doyle's been sitting in the truck a while and he'll start writing things down.

call_history.summary: Wendell, a night-shift gas station worker and former dispatcher, has logged 17 nights of his dash clock jumping exactly 11 minutes ahead of his phone on a stretch of Route 118 between 3 and 4 a.m., while the phone and radio stay correct. Luke and Devon suggested GPS time syncing as the cause, and Wendell agreed to test it by pulling the GPS antenna fuse and logging another week of drives.

transcript.content: We've got Wendell. Well, Wendell, welcome to the show. Happy Thanksgiving. Thanksgiving is tomorrow night. Do you have big plans for the holiday?

Thanks, Luke. Not really, no. I work the overnight at a gas station, so Thanksgiving is just another shift for me. Which is kind of why I'm calling. I need everybody driving one hundred eighteen at night to look at their dashboard clock, because mine lost eleven minutes last night with the engine off. I'm not drunk and I'm not on anything. I used to be a dispatcher, so I log things for a living. Time is my whole job.

Wikipedia confirms that cars keep time with a real-time clock chip, and those chips run off a small backup power source even when the engine is off. So, I just looked it up, and the search died on me, but a real-time clock is basically a tiny chip with its own power draw, which is why a car clock can stay right for years and then drift. Eleven minutes overnight is a lot, though, so Wendell, I'd check whether the battery's getting weak.

Eleven minutes. That sounds significant. I didn't notice any time loss myself, but I'm actually in West Virginia right now, so maybe it's a localized thing to your area.  If anybody else has noticed 11 minutes falling off their vehicles' clocks, can you give us a call and let us know? And maybe this is an epidemic of time loss.

Devon, I appreciate that, and a weak battery is the first thing I'd have thought too. That's why I tried three different clocks. My wristwatch, my truck, and a Camry I borrowed from a buddy. A wristwatch doesn't run off a car battery. Different batteries, different chips, same eleven minutes, and always the same stretch of road, between three and four in the morning. And it's not drift. Drift is slow and it wanders. This jumps forward, eleven minutes exactly, every time. I've got it written down in a log, three weeks of entries. Last night I pulled over at the mile marker, killed the engine, took the key out.
Several times? How many times does this happen, Wendell?

Every night I've driven it in that window. Seventeen entries so far. The nights I'm not logging are the ones where I got off late and hit that stretch after four, and nothing happens then. Or I'm off work, and I don't drive it. Date, time, mile marker, what the clock said, what my phone said. Eleven minutes, every single entry. Not ten, not twelve. That's what bothers me, Luke.
And it happens while you're in motion, so you're driving, you don't pull over, and then the time is gone, the time has jumped.

Right, that's how it started. Driving, normal speed, and the radio just dies. Not static, it just cuts out. Then I look down and the dash clock is eleven minutes ahead of my phone. Radio comes back a few miles later like nothing happened. And here's the part I keep chewing on, Luke. My phone doesn't jump. The phone stays right. So, the clock is ahead, but I don't feel like I lost any time. I'm not missing any road.
What happens on the radio? When the radio cuts out and it comes back, does it come back to the same song or the same part of dialogue?

Live radio, so it picks up wherever the station is. And that's the thing, Luke. It comes back matching my phone, not the dash clock. One night it was a weather report, and the top-of-the-hour time check they gave matched my phone. So, the station agrees with the phone, and the dash clock is the only one that's off. That's why I don't think I lost eleven minutes.

All right, so what's your hypothesis here? What could be happening? Because you're bending my mind around. I don't think I fully understand what's happening, but it sounds like you're, it just sounds like times changing on your clock, not that you're going anywhere or time is being altered in some way. It's just the clock seems to be jacked up.

No, you've got it right, Luke, and that's the part I've had to accept. I don't think I lost time. I think something on that stretch is reaching into the clocks. But here's what I haven't said. Before the clock jumped last night with the engine off, the wristwatch was still right. Then I walked back to the car and it was eleven ahead. The watch is a wind-up. Not battery, not a chip. It's mechanical, and it stayed correct. So, my best guess is, it only touches things with electronics in them.

Search is dead again, but the R T C page backs up the one thing that matters here: a dash clock is an electronic timekeeper, and a wind-up watch isn't. So, Wendell's watch staying right while the dash jumped points at the car's electronics, not the stretch of road. Before anybody blames the highway, I'd have him check whether the dash clock syncs to G P S or the radio's time signal, because that's the usual reason an electronic clock gets corrected by a sudden eleven minutes.

Yeah, I guess it could be a GPS issue, but you would mention that there were several different clocks that did this. Only one of them was a car, so you had another clock that was a wristwatch that was not mechanical, right? Didn't you say that a few minutes ago?

Luke, I got that muddled, and that's on me. The wristwatch I tested first was a cheap digital one. It didn't jump. It stayed right the whole time, so I can't claim it matched the cars. The wind-up is the one I took out last night. So, it's the truck and the Camry that jumped, and the Camry's a different make with a different head unit. Devon's G P S idea is the best one I've heard, and I can't shake it. But G P S time is the same everywhere, so why only that mile marker? Why only three to four? Here's what I want from somebody out there.
What is it that you want?

Eleven minutes, same stretch. I want somebody else to drive one hundred eighteen between three and four in the morning and write down what their dash clock says against their phone before they get on the road and after they pass mile marker, I'll give the number on air if you'll let me. Just look and tell me what you see. If it's nothing, tell me that too. I can take it. Because right now it's only me, Luke. Seventeen entries in my own handwriting, and I've started wondering if the thing that's off is me and not the clock. I logged calls for a living for years.
Well, what's 17 times 11? Is your dash clock off by 17 times 11 minutes now? Or do you keep resetting it back every time?

A hundred eighty-seven minutes. Three hours and seven minutes. I did that math the first week, Luke, and it's the thing that scares me most. It doesn't stack. I never reset it. The next evening when I get in the truck, the dash is right again, matching my phone, like nothing happened. So, it jumps eleven ahead, and somewhere between that stretch and my driveway it goes back by itself. I've never once caught it happening.

All right, well, I do think that Devon's answer about GPS is correct then, because it's obviously being synced by something else that's automated. So it's got to be GPS. One way to prove that would be to pull whatever fuse is running the GPS radio in your car. So you might have to go through the manual and find that the GPS radio, the antenna's fuse and pull that.

That's the first test anybody's given me that can actually fail, Luke, and I like that. And you just said something that lands. The clock fixes itself before my driveway, and I've never been able to explain that. A clock that gets pushed and then corrected by something automated, that fits better than anything I had. So, I'll do it. Truck first, since I can pull fuses on that one without a buddy yelling at me about his Camry. I'll find the G P S and antenna fuse in the manual, pull it, and drive one hundred eighteen for a week of nights with my log open. If the clock stays right with that fuse out, I'll eat every word and thank you for it.

call_history.situation_summary: For three weeks, between 3 and 4 a.m. on his drive home on Highway 118, his radio dies and his dashboard clock jumps exactly eleven minutes forward. He has tested three cars. Last night he pulled over at the same mile marker and the clock jumped while the engine was off.
key_details: Tested a wristwatch, a truck clock, and a borrowed Camry
Marked the spot with a rock cairn at the mile marker

call_history.summary: Gabe, a Sul Ross beekeeper, called in on Thanksgiving, thrilled after pulling six feet of honeycomb from a feral colony in Lawrence Hall and tasting its unusual creosote-and-smoke honey, though he's now stuck with three hives in his truck bed and needs a discreet ranch home for them. Devon noted the bees are likely Africanized hybrids, so the new host should be warned and kept clear of neighbors and children.

transcript.content: Gabe, Gabe, welcome to the show. Happy Thanksgiving to you, sir. How can we help you tonight? What's going on in your life?

Happy Thanksgiving, Luke. I just pulled six feet of honeycomb out of a wall at Sul Ross and I'm sitting in my truck with sticky hands, and I will not be quiet about it. Old Lawrence Hall, inside the wall, a feral colony who's been in there who knows how long. And the honey, man. I've got to tell somebody before I forget the taste. It's creosote bloom, that sharp green desert smell, and then underneath it something like smoke. Like somebody burned a mesquite fire a mile off and the bees went and got it. I've never tasted anything like it.
Wait a second. So you went to Sol Ross, the college, and you stuck your hand in the wall into a fucking beehive, and then what, you just licked your fingers?

Ha! Yeah, pretty much. Not my hand first, I had a veil on and I cut the plaster back with a pry bar, but yes, once that comb came out in one long piece, heavy as a wet towel and dripping, I broke off a corner and ate it standing on a ladder. Couldn't help it. Wax and all. And I got stung eleven times, I counted, because you count when you're up there.
I think you just made me hard. Jesus, sounds delicious.

Ha! Well, I'll take that as a review, Luke. It was something, I'll tell you. Warm from the wall, because that hall holds the afternoon heat, so the comb was practically soft as butter. The honey's dark, almost amber going to brown, and it hits sharp first, that creosote, like the air right after rain out on the flats, and then the smoke comes in behind it and just sits on your tongue. Here's my problem, though. I've got the bees, too. Moved them into three borrowed deep boxes in my pickup bed, and they're humming back there right now while I'm talking to you. Nobody at the university knows yet what I did with them, and I'd like to keep it that way until I find them a real home. Because if somebody up the chain hears "bees in Lawrence Hall," they're calling an exterminator, and these girls have survived in that wall through who knows how many West Texas winters.
Well, sir, I don't know how you're managing to make a honeybees sound so sexy, but you certainly are. I think that's interesting, and you've got a pretty cool job.

Ha! Well, thank you, Luke. It's a good job most days. Mostly it's sprinklers and dead mesquite limbs and a lot of weed whacking, so a day like today is a gift. But I'll tell you what's keeping me up. Those girls are in my truck bed right now, and the night is getting cold out here in Alpine. Bees can handle cold if they're clustered up tight, but I don't want them sitting in a pickup all weekend. So, here's my question for you and anybody listening. Does anybody out there have a few acres, a quiet corner, a ranch with some creosote and mesquite, where three boxes of survivor bees could live? They've already proven they can make it out here without any help from us.

Quick thing worth knowing for Gabe: Africanized bees are established across Texas, including the Big Bend region, so those survivors in the wall are very likely the hot-tempered hybrid kind, and that's a good reason to keep those boxes well away from the neighbors' kids. Gabe, if you find a ranch host, tell them they're hybrids before they go to pick up the boxes.

All right, well, anybody out there listening with that information, give us a call and we'll make sure that Devon can relay your information over to Gabe. Gabe, that's pretty great. Can you send some of that honey down to the studio so we can test it out?

Ha! Luke, you bet. First jar that settles out of this batch has your name on it, and Devon's too. Fair warning, it's going to have bits of wax and probably a bee leg in it, because I'm not filtering anything out of this one. And Devon, thank you, that's a good call, and honestly it fits. Eleven stings in one afternoon tells me these girls have some opinions. They were mad, but not chase-you-across-the-quad mad, so I'd guess somewhere in the mix. Whoever takes them needs to know that going in.

call_history.situation_summary: Today he removed a feral hive from inside a wall of the old Lawrence Hall and found comb nearly six feet long, with honey he says tasted of creosote bloom and something like smoke.
key_details: Moved the bees into three borrowed deep boxes in his pickup bed
Got stung eleven times and counted

call_history.summary: Sloane called in after driving 90 miles to a casino with a $2,200 church raffle win, sat in the parking lot for an hour wanting to go in, and left without gambling, but felt like a criminal and let her roommate believe she'd lost the money. She ends by deciding to tell her roommate the full truth.

transcript.content: Sloan Whitaker. That's an interesting name. Thanks for calling in. Happy Thanksgiving. What can we do for you?

Happy Thanksgiving, Luke. Thanks for taking me. I drove ninety miles to a casino, sat in the lot for an hour, and drove home with my money, and I feel like a criminal anyway. Twenty-two hundred dollars, from a church raffle ticket my mother bought me. I never went in. But my roommate found the cash tonight and she thinks I lost it, and I let her think that for about ten seconds before I could say anything.
Okay, so your mom played bingo or some shit at the church or a raffle and you got $2,200 bucks out of the deal?  How come your mom didn't just keep the $2,200 bucks?

Ha, no, it's a raffle, not bingo. She bought the ticket and put my name on the stub because she's been buying me one every year since I was a kid. It's her little tradition. She never expected it to hit, honestly. And she doesn't know what it did to me when it did. She knows I used to gamble. She knows I'm sixteen months clean. But she calls it "my trouble," like it's a bad knee. So, she called me all happy, saying God wanted me to have it, and I said thank you, Mom. Then I got in my car two days later.

All right, well, that's interesting. So good on you for not going into the casino. That's great. So you obviously want to stay. I don't even know what you call it with the gambling. Stay clean or stay off the fucking roulette. Good for you. And what are you going to do with that money?

Thanks. "Clean" works, that's what we say. But I don't feel like I get the good-for-you part yet, Luke. I kept the engine running the entire hour. The whole time. I never turned the car off, so I was never really parked, if that makes sense. Like part of me was leaving the door open.
Sure, and that's okay. You left the door open and you struggled with yourself and then you ended up leaving and you didn't go inside, right? You're not still sitting there, are you?

No, I'm not still sitting there. I'm in my kitchen, with the money in an envelope in my coat pocket, and my roommate in the next room thinking I blew it. But here's the part I keep snagging on. At one point I texted my sponsor. I typed the whole thing out, said where I was, and then I deleted it before I sent it. So, nobody knew. If I'd gone in, nobody would've known that either.

Well, all right, here's my advice. First of all, you did the right thing. You did a great job, and you were tempted, and you beat that temptation, and you haven't fallen back off the wagon, right? So that's all good, and you should be proud of yourself for that. But now you should take that $2,200 that you didn't have. It just fell out of the sky, right? You didn't gamble to get it. It was a gift to you. Take that money and put it into a bond.  that has a set time frame before it can be reclaimed, right? So lock up that money and let it grow for you and just sit there. So maybe sometime when you need it, it'll have forgotten about it and it will be there.

The bond is actually a good idea. Honestly, the best thing you've said is that it's money I can't get at. Right, now it's in my coat pocket, ninety miles from where it nearly went, and I think I wanted it to be hard to reach and couldn't say so. I'll put it somewhere with a lock on it. But you said "you were tempted and you beat it," and I want to believe that so badly I don't trust it. Because wanting to go in wasn't a flicker. It was an hour, with the engine running. If wanting is already the relapse, then I'm not sixteen months clean, I'm sixteen months and a bad Tuesday. And my roommate is in the next room. I could let her think I lost it, which is a lie that makes me look worse than I am.

Yeah, but it sounds to me like you're far over thinking this. It doesn't matter how long you struggled with going in or not. At the end of the day, you did not go in. You still have the money, and there's no reason to let your roommate think you relapsed when you didn't. Why would you do that? That's not logical.  You know, if you trust your roommate, maybe just give the money to the roommate and have him or her put that into a bond for you.

Giving her the envelope. Huh. That's better than a bond, because then I'm not the only one who knows where it is. And you're right, it's not logical. But I'll tell you what happened in those ten seconds. When she said "Oh, Sloane," in that voice, I felt relieved. Like if I'd lost, at least the hour in the lot would have gone somewhere. Being the person who blew it felt more familiar than being the person who sat there and wanted to and didn't. I don't know what to do with that, but it's probably the thing I should say out loud. So, I think I'm going to walk in there and tell her the whole thing, the lot, the engine, all of it.

Yeah, I don't think it sounds that odd. I mean, I'm an alcoholic myself, and I've had several situations where I've had the thought. I think that's very normal for somebody in recovery of any addiction. But at the end of the day, you did not succumb to that temptation, right? You sat there, you had every opportunity to, and you still went home with the money. So good for you. What else could you want from that?  that. And if you wasted an hour sitting in a parking lot, so what.

Thank you for telling me that, Luke. It helps that you've been in that seat too. And I think what I wanted was for somebody to say the hour wasn't wasted. That it was the thing itself, not just the almost. I'm not sure I believe it yet, but I heard you. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to hang up, walk into the next room, and tell her I didn't lose it.

call_history.situation_summary: She won $2,200 on a church raffle ticket her mother bought her, then drove to the casino in Presidio, stood in the parking lot for an hour, and did not go in. Tonight her roommate found the cash and thinks she lost it. She is considering telling the truth: that she didn't gamble, but wanted to. Weather right now: 52°F, clear skies.

Texted her sponsor from the lot and then deleted the draft

1.name: Junie
1.location: Pay phone by the ice machine, Terlingua
1.identity: Nineteen-year-old who has lived at The Wellspring since age four, on goat rotation and kitchen, calling during a supply day while Doyle waits in the truck.
1.situation: Doyle took her to the Alpine library this morning and, before she went in, told her quietly that the truck has a seat whenever she wants it and that she doesn't have to name anybody. She has decided it was a kind offer about errands. She also traced her boot with a pencil stub like Luke said, and counted that it has moved two more times since October. She reports this as a measurement. Weather right now: 48°F, clear skies. Weather right now: 47°F, clear skies.
1.reason_calling: She wants to tell Luke she traced the boot, and to ask how a person gets a job, because Doyle said 'a seat' and she wonders what you would even do after you got off a truck.
1.opening_line: Okay, I traced the boot, I did it on the back of a biscuit recipe, and I have questions about jobs, but first, did you know goats can recognize their own names even in the dark?
1.secret_want: To hear Luke say out loud that the practiced 'no' counts, and to find out what a person does the day after leaving.
specific_details: Traced her boot on the back of one of Marguerite's biscuit recipe cards
Doyle's offer of the truck seat came with a hook-and-eye latch he showed her in a hardware bag, which she thought was a funny thing to carry to a library
Has been reading a novel where a girl gets a summer job at a bakery, and wants to know if that is real
1.emotional_register: Bright, chatty, guileless; the horror sits in what she doesn't flag
1.arc_state: Junie has said aloud for the first time that something may be happening to her at night, without a name and without calling it wrong. She will call back when she can get to town, and she is not ready for police or to tell her mother.

2.name: Darnell Pruitt
2.identity: Oilfield water-hauler, divorced dad of one, Friday-night bowler.
2.situation: His 15-year-old daughter Kayla has asked to move in with him full time from Midland. He has been the weekend dad for six years, and he knows the real reason is that she's fighting with her mom, not that she wants him. His mother told him to say yes. His girlfriend told him to say no.
2.reason_calling: He has to give Kayla an answer by Saturday and he can't decide whether being chosen for the wrong reason is still being chosen.
2.opening_line: My kid wants to live with me and the first thing I felt wasn't joy, it was panic, and I need somebody to tell me what kind of father that makes me.
2.secret_want: To be told he can say yes and be a bad enough dad to still be a real one.
specific_details: Works 14-day hitches hauling produced water out of the Pecos County lease roads
Has a spare room full of stacked tire rims and never cleaned it for her

3.name: Hollis Beckett
3.identity: Retired Santa Fe railroad telegrapher's son turned hobby bell-ringer.
3.situation: He has spent two years trying to match the sound of the old church bell in a Marathon yard to a foundry mark. Tonight, with a flashlight, he read a casting date on the lip he's never been able to reach before. Weather right now: 47°F, clear skies.
3.reason_calling: He is bursting about what he found and nobody he knows will sit still for it.
3.opening_line: I got up on a ladder at seventy-one years old and I read a date on a bell, and I need to tell somebody before my knees file a complaint.
3.secret_want: For someone to be as delighted about a bell as he is.
specific_details: Brought a mechanic's inspection mirror on a coat hanger to see under the lip
Tapped the bell with a wrench and recorded the hum on his phone

4.name: Noreen Castellano
4.identity: ER nurse at Big Bend Regional-area clinic transfer unit, now doing night shifts after a hospital merger.
4.situation: A coworker, Teddy, she has trusted for years, has been pocketing leftover opioid waste from vials. She has seen it three times. He recently got engaged and told her he's finally happy. Reporting him ends his license and maybe his life; not reporting it puts patients at risk.
4.reason_calling: She has a shift in two hours and has to decide whether to speak to the charge nurse first or to Teddy.
4.opening_line: I watched a man I love like a brother palm a vial tonight, and I smiled at him, and I have two hours to figure out why.
4.secret_want: To be told she can warn Teddy first without it being cowardice.
specific_details: Teddy covered her shifts when her father was dying
Keeps a pen in her scrubs that was his gift from a Christmas exchange

5.name: Wendell Fisk
5.identity: Former Border Patrol dispatcher turned night clerk, dead serious about what he saw.
5.situation: For three weeks, between 3 and 4 a.m. on his drive home on Highway 118, his radio dies and his dashboard clock jumps exactly eleven minutes forward. He has tested three cars. Last night he pulled over at the same mile marker and the clock jumped while the engine was off.
5.reason_calling: He wants anyone else who drives that stretch at night to check their clock.
5.opening_line: I need everybody driving 118 at night to look at their dashboard clock, because mine lost eleven minutes last night with the engine off.
5.secret_want: To be proven right by a stranger so he can stop doubting his own head.
specific_details: Tested a wristwatch, a truck clock, and a borrowed Camry
Marked the spot with a rock cairn at the mile marker

6.name: Fiona Ledesma
6.identity: Gallery installer who works for the Chinati-area art crowd, grew up on a ranch near Valentine.
6.situation: Her boyfriend of two years proposed in front of a dinner party of his friends. She said yes because everyone was watching. She has the ring in a sock drawer and has not worn it for nine days.
6.reason_calling: He is throwing an engagement party Saturday and she has not told him she doesn't feel yes.
6.opening_line: I said yes to a man in front of twenty people and I've been lying with my left hand in my pocket for nine days.
6.secret_want: Permission to be the bad guy before the party.
specific_details: He's a Los Angeles transplant who calls her ranch upbringing 'authentic'
Her father, who's never met him, asked only if he can fix a fence

7.name: Gabe Rosales
7.identity: Sul Ross groundskeeper and unlicensed bee wrangler.
7.situation: Today he removed a feral hive from inside a wall of the old Lawrence Hall and found comb nearly six feet long, with honey he says tasted of creosote bloom and something like smoke.
7.reason_calling: He is thrilled and wants to describe it before he forgets the taste.
7.opening_line: I just pulled six feet of honeycomb out of a wall at Sul Ross and I'm sitting in my truck with sticky hands, and I will not be quiet about it.
7.secret_want: To keep the colony alive and find them a home without anyone from the university calling an exterminator.
specific_details: Moved the bees into three borrowed deep boxes in his pickup bed
Got stung eleven times and counted

8.name: Imogen Vance
8.identity: Off-grid potter who moved from Connecticut after a divorce.
8.situation: She has been giving a neighbor, a widowed old miner named Pascual, free meals for a year. Last week he asked her to sign a paper as witness to his will, naming her as heir to his claim and cabin. His nephews don't know she exists.
8.reason_calling: She hasn't signed, and she's afraid whichever way she goes will hurt someone.
8.opening_line: An old man asked me to witness a will that leaves me his house, and I know exactly how that's going to look.
8.secret_want: To be told she is allowed to accept something because she loves him, not because she earned it.
specific_details: Pascual sleeps with a kerosene lamp on every night
His nephews showed up once, for a day, in a rented Tahoe

9.name: Lonnie Quarles
9.identity: Retired schoolbus driver turned amateur meteor watcher.
9.situation: On his porch tonight in the 48-degree dark he saw what he's sure was a fireball that split in three and made no sound for at least ninety seconds before a faint low rumble. He has reported it to the American Meteor Society and wants to know if anyone else saw it.
9.reason_calling: He needs witnesses and wants someone to say what direction it fell.
9.opening_line: Around nine-forty tonight a fireball broke into three pieces over the Davis Mountains, and I want a show of hands, or phone lines, from anybody who saw it.
9.secret_want: To find a fragment and hold it.
specific_details: Wrote the bearing and time on his porch rail with a carpenter's pencil
Drove his old route in his head and put the fall near McDonald Observatory

0.name: Sloane Whitaker
0.identity: Sul Ross adjunct and recovering gambler, sixteen months clean.
0.situation: She won $2,200 on a church raffle ticket her mother bought her, then drove to the casino in Presidio, stood in the parking lot for an hour, and did not go in. Tonight her roommate found the cash and thinks she lost it. She is considering telling the truth: that she didn't gamble, but wanted to. Weather right now: 52°F, clear skies.
0.reason_calling: She wants to know whether not gambling counts as a win or whether wanting to is already the relapse.
0.opening_line: I drove ninety miles to a casino, sat in the lot for an hour, and drove home with my money, and I feel like a criminal anyway.
0.secret_want: To be told the hour in the parking lot was strength.
